utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you are General Sir Martin Garrod, who, when you finished your first career as the Officer Commanding the British Royal Marines, a three-star General; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not embracing the notion of retirement, you obtained employment for the ECMM and succeeded J.P. Thebault as the head of the centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April '94 you were appointed Chief Of Staff of the European Union Administrator in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were subsequently an European Union Special Envoy in Mostar until December of 1996?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since then, you have been working in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Just recently in Kosovo. I spent some more time in Bosnia with the Office of the High Representative, but the last six months in Kosovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May the witness, incidentally, have a copy of his summary before him. And there are small stacks of exhibits. May he have one of those before him as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with the summary first. Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your years in Bosnia, how did the Bosnian Croats regard President Tudjman of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, they regarded him in great -- with great honour. They referred to him as "our President." The Croats carried the Croatian passports, they voted in the Croatian elections, and they sang the Croatian national anthem. So in other words, as far as they were concerned, President Tudjman was their President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a crossover from post-holders in one entity to another; for example, Susak?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, there were a number of Herzegovinian Croats in the Croatian Government, and most notably, of course, the Defence Minister, Gojko Susak. But there were a number of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dario Kordic, in summary, what was his position? As you understood it.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: My understanding was that Dario Kordic then was Vice-President of the HDZ, and also Vice-President of the HVO. He was, as far as I was concerned, the leading Croat political figure in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one word about the -- one sentence about the HVO. Responsive to this two-part question, was the HVO completely a military organisation? And if the answer is no, is there any analogous organisation better known to those of us in other countries that you can liken it to?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, the Hrvatsko Vijece Obrane, the Croat Defence Council, was by its name the Defence Council, but it did have wider responsibilities. For example, Jadranko Prlic, who is the de facto Prime Minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, was the President of the HVO, and his Deputy, Kresimir Zubak, was the Vice-President of the HVO. So while it was essentially a Defence Council, it did have wider governmental responsibilities. Later on, the HVO came synonymous with the Croat Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For those of us, for example, from Western European countries, is there any analogous body typically to be found in our States, or not?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Not in the initial days. I don't think there is any -- I can't see any really comparison with an organisation in any other -- in any Western European or western country. But, as I say, eventually it became purely synonymous with the Army, the defence side, the HVO. But in the early days it had wider responsibilities, as I've explained, with Jadranko Prlic being President of the HVO, and also de facto Prime Minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can deal with paragraph 6 very briefly. You got to know or know of Anto Valenta, you saw him in his office, which had maps, and you knew about the book he had written?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. I'd had several meetings with Anto Valenta, mainly in his office in Vitez, and he was -- he was an expert on ethnic breakdown in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and indeed had written at least one book, maybe more, which he was delighted to discuss with anyone who would listen about his views on how Bosnia should have been divided up into three ethnic entities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time in Central Bosnia, did you form a view about how Central Bosnian Croats may have viewed their Herzegovinian neighbours, and compared their lot, one with another?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: There was certainly a view, which was expressed to me more than once and sometimes with a degree of bitterness, that the Central Bosnian Croats -- and after all, there had been a larger number of Croats in Central Bosnia than down in Herzegovina -- had been somewhat forsaken by their Herzegovina colleagues for the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Yes, I had that view on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which sector of Croats was there more enthusiasm for the Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, the feeling was definitely down in the south, certainly in the Mostar area and spreading right throughout the southern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was there that the feeling for -- the enthusiasm for the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was the strongest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 20th of October of 1993, did you receive a report from William Stutt about six ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. I received a report that six ABiH soldiers had been arrested near an HVO checkpoint near Stupni Do. Stupni Do had been a Muslim enclave south of Vares which had been, up until then, virtually untouched by the fighting in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll take paragraph 10 first for generalities. How many times altogether did you meet Kordic, at his headquarters, do you calculate?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It's hard to be precise. It must have been at least four or five times, maybe more. My meetings with Dario Kordic were mainly in Busovaca, in his house there, which was colloquially known as the Eagle's Nest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a place in the town or out in the country?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It was about two or three kilometres south, south-east -- wrong -- yes, south-east of Busovaca, along a small road in a wooded area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met him, was he typically alone or typically accompanied, and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: He was -- there was always HVO guards in the area of the house. He was -- I don't recall him ever being alone, and the person who was -- invariably lived with him was the secretary of the HVO, Ignac Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was Kordic dressed when you met him?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was invariably dressed in a camouflage uniform, but I do not recall -- if he was badges of rank, I do not recall what badges of rank he might have been wearing. But it was invariably a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you to ask him about rank and matters of that sort?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Strange enough, the subject of rank never really occurred to me as a question. At that time, of course, not only in the HVO but also in the Bosnian Army, the civil side and the -- the political side and the military side were very, very much intertwined, and so one was dealing with political leaders on military matters and military leaders on political matters. And so rank did not -- was not of great significance. The important point was the influence and stature that a man held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness now have a pile of exhibits, as may the Chamber. Perhaps the usher could have a separate pile to lay on the ELMO for the public to read, as appropriate. If the witness can simply have the pile himself. If the Usher could have a separate pile, then. There may be, I think, some three exhibits already produced that I will ask the witness about, and if the Registrar hasn't got the numbers, we'll provide the numbers to her for them to be extracted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first document, 1255, a Zenica daily report for the 21st of October. Does this record on the second page, in the middle of the page, a meeting that you had with Dario Kordic and also Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a meeting first with Anto Valenta and then a second meeting with Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this one occurred in that same mountain or hillside or hilly --

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- chalet, which I think was --

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: The chalet in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Called what?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: The Eagle's Nest, it was known as.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We can see from the report that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which bit are you referring to, please, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second page, middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "He then went on to say the Croats could leave Zenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He first of all said that a military solution was not in the interests of the state, as both sides were equally matched. He said that he expected a major offensive in the Lasva Valley, aimed at seizing the explosives factory in Vitez. He went on to say the HVO defenders were well armed and then said, we see in the middle of the page, that the Croats would leave Zenica and start their lives again, as they do not feel protected there. Did you ask him whether the people would return if a peace plan were to be agreed?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask whether he thought the Croats would return to Zenica. But he said he thought that a few would, but once one had left one's area of one's own free will, it's difficult to return. Some would remain if a peace plan would be agreed, but fewer than before the war, and it would depend very much on how they were treated by the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to take you through all the entries here, but at the very foot of this page that we're looking on, looking at, he said that he deplored the fact that the Muslims used the supply of water and power as weapons of war and said that the Croats would never do such a thing?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. We were having considerable difficulty in the Vitez and Novi Travnik/Nova Bila area about the supply of water and power which was being used. At that time, the Croats were suffering in Vitez from a lack of power and water, and this was a constant problem that we were facing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any comment on the protestation that he made, that the Croats would never do such a thing?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, yes. Of course, inevitably in Bosnia I found that one of the biggest problems that we faced was linkages, linkages. One side would not do this until the other side did that. And this question of power and water and so on was all part of this linkage business, and it was a battle that we were continually fighting, to try to get rid of the linkages from unravelling difficult problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would go, please, to the last page of this exhibit, the second paragraph, or first fresh paragraph, it may be. Did you summarise or was there summarised from this meeting this passage: "The meetings with Mr. Valenta and Mr. Kordic today were of interest, as they reflect the views of the two most influential Croat civil leaders in Central Bosnia"?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just waiting --

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Although it is not, perhaps, surprising, their views were remarkably similar on a number of topics. As they must undoubtedly see each other regularly and discuss these and similar subjects together, they could almost have been speaking with one voice." Did that judgement hold good just for this meeting, or for all your time there?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: No. I think, throughout my time there, I realised that there was, or I appreciated that there was an extremely close link between Mr. Dario Kordic and Mr. Anto Valenta. And there is no doubt about it; they probably -- because they discussed these things on a very regular basis, and indeed with higher levels in the Croat hierarchy. But their views were absolutely in line throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We now move to the information that you first received about the massacre of Stupni Do. When did you receive that, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: We -- I think it was on the 24th of October we first started receiving reports of a massacre, a possible massacre in Stupni Do. But at that stage it was not confirmed, because the HVO commander of the Bobovac Brigade, in Vares, Emil Harah, had denied entry to Stupni Do to all international agencies, including UNPROFOR, which in that area was the NordBat, the Norwegian battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear reports of changes in people of authority in the Vares area?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. We received reports on the 25th that Emil Harah had been replaced by Kresimir Bozic, but that Ivica Rajic appeared to be in charge in Vares. So it would appear as though there had been a change in the HVO command on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that day, did you have a meeting with Dario Kordic about something else?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. I'd already planned a meeting with Dario Kordic to discuss a particular problem that we faced, and this was the seizure of two Medivac helicopters belonging to the ABiH, which had been seized down in Medugorje. So I had a meeting with him on that day, specifically to discuss the helicopters, but of course, in the light of the circumstances, I, of course, raised the subject of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you express an attitude at that meeting about linkage, and if you can't remember --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- tendered, 126 --

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Right. Right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps this one can be laid on the ELMO, and then the witness can see it as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document that's been produced by an earlier witness. If we look towards the foot of the first page, we see, as part of your report on the meeting, that Kordic said he fully agreed there should be not any linkage between Medivac flights and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just raise one objection to the phraseology of that question. The question was: This was Sir Martin's report. Apparently, this report was prepared by a gentleman by the name of Jeff Beaumont. It's not actually Sir Martin's report at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a report is prepared by someone else, how, if at all, would you have contributed to its content?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: The way I would contribute was, for example, if I went to a report like this, if I went to a meeting like this, I would then go to my own room afterwards and type up a copy of the report on my laptop computer, transfer it to disk, hand it over to my Deputy, who was Jeff Beaumont. Then that would be inserted into the main report. So I would have an input, as required, into our main daily report and, when necessary, I would produce what were called HRC's, comments, at the end of the report, if I felt there was anything particular I wished to bring to the attention of our headquarters in Zagreb. So a report like this would have been typed by me, and then -- almost certainly typed by me, and then put on disk, to be inserted into the main report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And so we see, at the foot of the first page, the reference to there being no linkage, and Kordic agreeing to that?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. He agreed there should be no linkage between the Medivac flights and the POWs. And he said he would take -- use his authority, telephone Mate Boban, General Praljak, who was then the Commander of the HVO, Military Command of the HVO, and Petkovic, who was his Chief Of Staff immediately after I had left, with a view to getting the helicopters released. To him, clearly, the continual evacuation from the Nova Bila hospital was most important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he then questioned about Stupni Do, in light of the suspicion of atrocities? Did he say that he had telephoned General Petkovic? The second page, please, of the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would appreciate it if the Prosecution would not lead on this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's in the report. So they can't be criticised for reading out what's in the report, and then asking the witness whether it's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can, General. And one thing: The long pause reflects the fact that if one listens to the French around one's neck, then we can ensure that we don't burden the interpreters too much.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not at all. So if we look at the document, the foot of the first page. Questioned about Stupni Do, did he say that he had telephoned General Petkovic in Kiseljak and that General Petkovic had told him nothing bad had happened; a lot of houses were burning, and a lot of soldiers, in and out of uniform, had been killed, but most of the civilians had moved out and were now in Vares?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. He responded immediately and said that as soon as he had heard about Stupni Do, he had telephoned General Petkovic, who I understand at that time was in Kiseljak, and who he said had told him what you have just -- what you have stated. That is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to the next paragraph, looking at the first part of the next paragraph. Did he say that Muslim allegations had to be checked and that they were making a lot of excuses for their attack on Kopjari, while at the same time accusing the HVO of the attack on Stupni Do? And did he say that he did not believe there had been a deliberate attack on civilians, although there may have been some who stayed in their houses and did not want to surrender?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. He referred to a village called Kopjari. We had checked out Kopjari, and nothing of significance had happened in Kopjari. He stressed that he used the words, "Speaking as a soldier, and a human being, I severely condemn atrocities committed by any side." And I think that's all I can say about that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, finally, his comment on Vares was that in Vares there were good relations with two BiH corps, and he suggested that there were Muslims who didn't like that and were determined to stir up enmity between the HVO and the BiH?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, that was certainly a view. Certainly in the north in Tuzla, in the Tuzla area, with the two BiH corps, there were good working relationships between the Armija of Tuko [phoen], commanded by a Bosniak general and the HVO in the Tuzla region. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to reinforce what you explained to us about the form at of these reports. If we go to the last page but one, we see, under HRC's assessment, your overall assessment being made on this day. And if we then turn over to the last page, where you've summarised matters, you end in this way. Speaking of linkages, in the last sentence you say: "At least Dario Kordic today deplored such linkages, promising to use his authority to unblock the helicopter issue. We will see if his authority carries sufficient weight."

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, it was a very clear statement by Dario Kordic that he himself, after our discussion, deplored these linkages, linking one issue with another, so that there was a complete log jam. And he promised to unblock, do his best to unblock the helicopter issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document is the -- the next document in the stack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will you just pause a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to the next document: Despite the promises, how long was it before the helicopters were released?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It took a good five months before those helicopters were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document, 1266, is the daily report for the 26th of October, again prepared by Jeff Beaumont, and if we turn to the second page of this document, do we see an entry at the foot of the page built on a report to you from William Stutt?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, and this particularly concerned the report that General Petkovic had apparently sent two documents to his subordinate units, declaring a ceasefire in the Vares area and directing that three of the Croat officials in the Vares area were to be replaced: Ante Pejnovic, the President of the HVO; Zvonko Duznovic, the Chief Of Security; and Ivica Gavran, Commander of the Civilian Police and member of the Presidency. And we had already discovered that the Commander of the Bobovac Brigade had already changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any suggestion or implication that these changes of appointments may have been connected to what happened in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It is not -- it was not actually stated as such, but there is no doubt at all that that was the clear inference, that these changes were made as a result of the Stupni Do incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in fact, did you have any other evidence that those named people who were being replaced were, in fact, connected to what had happened at Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: No. At that stage, I did not, no. I did not have those particular names, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn over the page just to check that there's nothing else that we want to raise. The report goes on to say: "Even if these documents turn out to be authentic, it still leaves doubt over aims and objectives and how high up the military chain of command orders were given for the attack on Stupni Do"?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. That was the feeling that we had at the time. It was unclear to us where -- how high up the chain of command orders had been given for that attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can deal with paragraph 19 briefly. We've heard evidence about it already. I think on the 27th of October, Nordbat gained access to Stupni Do. They found the burnt village, bodies -- men, women and children -- and indications of torture; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is correct. It had taken some time to get into Stupni Do, but, as you say, on the 27th finally NordBat did gain access. And one of our teams, Victor 4, I think it was, went in with them to discover these terrible scenes in Stupni Do itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document, then, is 1284.1. Now, this is a report dated the 3rd of November, but the entry to which it relates occurred on the -- or the incident to which the entry relates occurred on the 30th of October, and this is a report of your own, I think.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. The reason why it was dated two or three days after the event was because, as you can see, it's a fairly long report, and life was busy and it took two or three days to actually type it all up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go to the second page, at the top of the page, in capital letters, we can see that there was a meeting between -- who is HOM?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That's the Head Of Mission, Head Of Mission of the EC Monitor Mission based in Zagreb. At that time, it was the Belgian Presidency of the EU, and the Head of the Mission was Ambassador de Baans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I was present at all these meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through all of it -- sorry, I must stop. I'm not going to go through all of it because the text is available to be read, but at the foot of the second page, paragraph 5, did Kordic say that the victims of Stupni Do had become the aggressors? I beg your pardon. Did he say the victims had become aggressors, and was then asked about Stupni Do by the Head Of Mission, asked if what had happened would not damage the image of the Croats, to which he replied that the CRHB would condemn any atrocity, but added that Muslim Radio was believed, whatever it said, and that no one took notice of Muslim atrocities, going on to say some houses had been burned, that there might have been people in those houses, but that he couldn't believe the HVO would have deliberately killed civilians, adding that suitable action would be taken after an inquiry or the inquiry was completed and that no one would be protected? Was, to your knowledge, any inquiry ever completed, that you learned about?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, we had similar assurances, both from Mate Boban and from Jadranko Prlic, but to my knowledge no inquiry was conducted by the Croat authorities and no one was ever brought to justice for the attack and massacre in Stupni Do. Nor did I ever see a report from Croat sources stating what they believed had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page we see, at paragraph 8, Kordic deploring the fact that Muslims were using power and water for military purposes, explaining the position about Nova Bila hospital and shortages of fuel and food, and saying, on the subject of the helicopters, that he had made telephone calls, giving an explanation for why, perhaps, they hadn't been released and saying they were going to be released; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is so, that is so. Yes, I believe that even he -- I believe that he himself, suddenly from his turn, was optimistic that these helicopters would be released, which were, of course, crucial to the medical evacuation system -- reciprocal medical evacuation system that had been set up between the Croats and the Bosniaks from Nova Bila down to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I also ought to draw your attention to paragraph 6 on the same page, where he expressed certain views about -- and the Chamber can read it themselves -- the Islamic fundamentalist direction of Izetbegovic and saying that the religious leaders stood for a Jihad and were forcing him, that is, Izetbegovic, to seize as much territory as he could, including Vitez, Busovaca, Travnik and Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you moving from that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got one other short passage to go through and then I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to deal with that, and then I've got a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 9 of the document, we see, at the foot of the page, something of your meeting with Mate Boban. Is this a report of the meeting with Boban?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, this is a report of a meeting that I attended together with Ambassador de Baans, with Mate Boban and his close advisor, Vladislav Pogarcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we see paragraph 6 on the topic of Stupni Do, you being told that all those who were killed were soldiers and that anyone found guilty of misconduct would be disciplined, at the same time being told about the village of Kopljari which had apparently been wiped off the face of the earth, the Muslims planning to attack Vares?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This was -- he stated that his information was that all those who had been killed were soldiers, and of course this was manifestly not so, but that disciplinary action would be taken against anyone found guilty. And he again raised the subject of Kopljari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, would you go back, please, to that meeting with HOM, pages 2 and 3 of the document. One of the matters you may be able to help us about -- I don't know -- is the relationship between Messrs. Kordic, Kostroman and Valenta. Now, it appears, from your report of the meeting, that Mr. Kordic was the one doing the talking on the Croatian side. Would that, in fact, be right?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely, Your Honour. Mr. Kordic was the prime figure. Anto Valenta was considerably older. He was more or less, shall I use the word, a father figure, whereas I would guess Dario Kordic then was in his early 30s. Anto Valenta must have been in his 60s, at least. He was a different generation and had a different, really, advisory role, whereas the leader was Dario Kordic, so it was inevitable that he would take the lead in the discussions with Ambassador de Baans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And was that what happened at the other meetings that you went to, Kordic taking the lead?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, yes, certainly. I did not go to many meetings where both Kordic and Valenta were present, but when I did, it would be Kordic who would be leading, and, indeed, leading also at a meeting that I recall with Blaskic, the General. So Kordic was in the driving seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. At some stage, it would be helpful to know the age of Mr. Anto Valenta. No doubt you can get some evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure we'll be able to establish that, probably from his book, but we'll be able to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other thing from this document which we can summarise. It's on page 9, paragraph 7. Boban also dealt with the helicopters and promised to have them released; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. Boban, yes, he was clearly somewhat irritated about being tackled about the helicopters, but he said that he would, and he said that he would go down to Medjugorje personally to get them released. But, of course, it took another five months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a reference, actually, in paragraph 7 -- I don't know if you can help with this -- to his saying that when 12,000 Croats were forced to leave from Kakanj to Vares, they received no help from the ECMM, UNPROFOR or the ICRC, and had to pay the Serbs to escape to the south. And then there is a quotation about the helicopters that had brought the HOM to the meeting. Can you just give us the setting for that?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid I cannot give details about the move of the -- of the Croats from Kakanj to Vares, because I am not certain as to when that actually happened, but he was certainly in a very difficult mood that day, and he produced this barb against the Head Of the Mission by saying that it was only because of the helicopters that we had gone to see him at all, which, of course, was manifestly not so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also, I think, saw Prlic. We can see that in summary. Did he tell you -- that's at the last pages of this document. Did he tell you that the government had suspended all possibly involved HVO Commanders?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And he said they had suspended all the Commanders and had ordered General Petkovic to carry out an investigation. And he also said the Minister Of Law had been instructed to start a special commission, looking into all crimes, possible crimes, including Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The top of page 10, paragraph 2. We've already dealt with paragraph 23 of the summary. And I can go on to the next document, 1275, which relates to the 31st of October. This document is prepared, I think, by William Stutt. And is it a report, a daily summary report from him for you?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see that he, I think, met Bozic, Kresimir Bozic. And was that with you as well?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: No. That was himself meeting Bozic separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's said to be nervous, this is the first page, and saying that he had been promoted to take over a new position. The comment there is that this was believed to be a piece of scene-setting or serious scene-setting. Was that Mr. Stutt's judgement or yours, or a collective judgement?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: This is Stutt's comment in his report, but I would agree with the sentiment in that it seemed strange that this sudden new appointment had been effected the day after the massacre in Stupni Do. The coincidence seems considerable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn over to the second page, paragraph 5. You see: HCC was given the transcript of evidence taken by a NordBat military policeman of a Muslim taken prisoner in Vares, two days before the Stupni Do massacre, and the contemporary assessment that was built on that source, and maybe others, from NordBat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. From NordBat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that assessment, in summary, was that, prior to the massacre, Muslims in Vares were arrested and taken to the schools, that the massacre was by the HVO extremists from Kakanj, although intelligence was certainly required; there were reports of HVO Vares soldiers assisting Muslims and helping some of them to escape. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The clear understanding that we had was that the attack was done by the HVO from Kakanj and Kiseljak, not the HVO from Vares. And there clearly was a difference between the two, between the HVO from Kakanj and Kiseljak, and Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The contemporary analysis went on to reveal that in the days following the attack, Vares was controlled by Kakanj HVO troops, and incarcerated Muslims were beaten and subjected to the forced singing of Croatian songs; and that following the massacre, three senior civilians in the Vares Government were replaced, although the Muslims remained prisoners; and NordBat, on their investigation, found some 22 badly beaten prisoners, who they moved to another location.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to Valenta's book, his date of birth is the 28th of January, 1937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before we part from document 1275, I think Bozic made it clear, this is on the first page, that his brigade, or the brigade of which he was then in charge, might have to withdraw further south, but that Vares would be defended to the last man. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Yes, that is so. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go then to the summary, paragraph 26. Were you informed by NordBat of their evacuation of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. They informed us that they were evacuating about 40 Muslims daily to the Breza area, which is further south, and around 200 Muslims in Vares had sought refuge in NordBat because raping and looting was a nightly occurrence in Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the date of that information from NordBat?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it was the 2nd of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that day were you due to have a meeting with Kresimir Bozic?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I was not, but the head of the co-ordination centre, William Stutt, was due to meet Bozic. But he was in fact told he should deal with Zvonko Dusnovic, who was the Chief Of Security, who was supposed to have been dismissed by General Petkovic following the Stupni Do massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The effect of that, on your attitude towards these dismissals and replacements, was what?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, it certainly cast doubt on the seriousness of the HVO leaders to replace the Commanders, and to undertake the investigations that they had promised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 2nd and 3rd of November. Please tell us what happened, in summary.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: On the 2nd of November, the ABiH attacked Vares. It was a bloodless operation, because the HVO had departed rapidly and headed north to Dastansko. And on the 3rd of November, we stated that the HVO had abandoned Vares, released all prisoners, set the headquarters of the HVO on fire, and heading to Dastansko, which is just about one kilometre west of the border with the Bosnian-Serb-Army-controlled territory, to the north-east of Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go to Vares soon thereafter?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I went up with William Stutt the next day to find the ABiH fully under -- fully in control of the whole Vares area. It was -- my guess is there was a lot of alcohol, because there was a lot of wild and indiscriminate machine-gun firing throughout the town. And we met the Commanding Officer of the Armija, who told us that the occupation of Vares was a direct result of Stupni Do. Though, of course, there was considerable strategic gain, as far as the Armija was concerned, because, with the capture of Vares, they could now travel from Tuzla to Gornji Vakuf without passing through any HVO pockets. So it was a considerable strategic advantage to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a report later that concerned a man called Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. On the 7th of November, one of our team attended a tripartite meeting in Kiseljak to discuss a refugee problem. Following a half-an-hour propaganda speech by the HVO Commander, Ivica Rajic, the UNHCR representative walked out of the meeting, which prompted Rajic to threaten him by saying, "Don't ever show up in Kiseljak again."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May the witness, please, see the exhibit that's already been tendered, 1293.1. This document, dated the 9th of November, is prepared by, if you look at the last page, is it Aage Terp and Gerard van der Elshout?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Those are the -- yes, the Operation Officers of the Headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Insofar as relevant, on the first page it deals with the report of a meeting with Dario Kordic. This was Stutt's meeting, I think?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we see there, two-thirds of the way down the page under paragraph number 2, is that Kordic said that Rajic had given way to stress. Your understanding of that was what?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: My understanding of that was that what Kordic was saying was that Rajic, by attacking the UNHCR representative of the meeting, had given -- had been overcome by stress, which was the reason why he threatened him by saying, "Don't ever show up in Kiseljak again." That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was, if not apologising for, in any event, seeking to explain the behaviour of this man, Rajic?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive, shortly thereafter, reports of a change in Rajic's position?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. On the 11th of November, we heard that Rajic was no longer in command in Kiseljak, and had been temporarily replaced, following instructions by General Petkovic. We also, although I didn't see it myself, one of our team reported that the Croatian press had said that Ivica Rajic had been removed on the orders of Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next paragraph 34 is capable of being supported by an exhibit already tendered, but I don't need to call for it. Is it right, General, that on the 16th of November, you recall a meeting between Philip Watkins and Slobodan Lovrenovic, Boban's press advisor?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. This was at a time when the Croatian -- there were a lot of changes in the hierarchy of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the establishment of a Presidential Council, and, therefore, a number of the Vice-President positions disappeared. But to me it did not, in any way, affect my estimation of the significance and important role which Dario Kordic played in the hierarchy of the Croats. There were many changes, and it was an evolving situation; the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and then the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Councils, House of Representatives, and so on. But these various changes did not really matter to me so much. What mattered was the significant part that individuals had played or were still playing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that same day did you learn of a change in the position of Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. General Slobodan Praljak, we heard that day, had been relieved by General Ante Roso. And I, at the time, assessed that General Praljak's departure was due to a -- well, the lack of military success of the HVO, but also there were other recent factors which may well have played a part, such as Stupni Do, the loss of Vares, and indeed the destruction of the Stari Most, the old bridge in Mostar, which took place on the 9th of November, just one week before this changeover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same day, did you have a report of the access or denial of access to Dastansko?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. One of our teams reported that they were denied access to Dastansko by the HVO, but heard that the Bosnian-Serb Army were supplying the HVO with ammunition and had as many as 8,000 soldiers along the confrontation line. Dastansko was extremely close to the border with the Serb-occupied territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little later, did Darko Gelic and Blaskic confirm to Stutt that Kordic's position was different?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: No, they confirmed that Kordic would remain a Vice-President of Mate Boban, though it appeared that Valenta had no position. The explanation was that the appointment of Kordic took time because he could not attend the last assembly meeting. But we concluded -- I concluded that Kordic's position remained strong, while Valenta was fading from the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I think that there's nothing on the next document that's been tendered through an earlier witness that I need trouble the Chamber with in detail, but by the 15th of December, despite what you were told by, for example, Philip Watkins about Kordic's nominal or formal position as a member of the House of Representatives, what was the overall assessment?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, again, I did not take -- read too much into this, because at this stage they were forming the Presidential Council and Kordic subsequently became a member of that council, and so the Vice-Presidents had gone. It was a little bit complicated to follow all the changes and manoeuvrings, but I had no doubt in my mind at all that Dario Kordic's position remained very strong and he had great influence and power within the hierarchy of the Croats. And there was also the additional factor which may be true. The reason given by Lovrinovic, Mate Boban's spokesman, was that a full-time presence in Mostar might be required for a position in government and it might give out the wrong message to use, as he, in his words -- in his words, extracting someone who is a war hero in Central Bosnia and bringing him down to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same day, which the tendered document would, I think, show to be the 15th of December, did you receive information from Maric and also from Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. Maric from Busovaca, HVO President, had said that Kordic had refused a position as a Minister in order better to serve the Croats in Central Bosnia. And Blaskic, who saw Stutt earlier that day, made it clear that, in his mind, there was no doubt at all of Kordic's importance -- Dario Kordic's importance for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Coming to the end of the year, and I think it's on the 28th of December, according to the document tendered by another witness, did Darko Gelic give information about Kordic's position?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. Darko Gelic, who was the Liaison Officer with the HVO in Vitez, said that Kordic had a new function, and that was of Assistant Chief Of Staff to General Roso, which would have put him directly number three in the military hierarchy, with General Roso at the top; General Petkovic, Chief Of Staff; and then Dario Kordic, Assistant Chief Of Staff, in the straight military hierarchy, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 1344, please, which is the next one on the stack, this being a document, I think, prepared by Michael O'Donnell. Tell us about him.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Mike O'Donnell?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: He was one of our -- he was our Operations Officer for a while, Irish Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the first page of this document, we see this entry under the political situation, paragraph 1. It says that: "The ECMM met Ivo Tokic, President of the Municipality of Tomislavgrad, and the status of Boban was discussed. Tokic believed that the European Union was contributing to rumours of Boban's replacement after presenting the 14-point document to President Tudjman." Just tell us about that, if you can.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, this was Mijo Tokic. I think there must be a slight error here. Mijo Tokic was the President of the Municipality of Tomislavgrad. We were aware that there was a 14-point document which had been put to Dr. Franjo Tudjman. We had not seen it, we had not seen it, but Tokic told Watkins that this document stated that progress in the peace talks depended on Mate Boban being replaced. But as I say, I have never seen that 14-point document, and this is purely information from Mijo Tokic. But he seemed convinced that there were moves ahead to perhaps replace Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you were concerned, was there any truth in the suggestion that the European Union was contributing to the rumours or not, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't know, I don't know, I don't know. As I say, one tended, I'm afraid, to be, in Central Bosnia, to be slightly out of the information loop as far as international events were concerned, and so I could not say whether that was true or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zoran Mijic, mayor of Busovaca, make a suggestion on that day?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. He had suggested that -- or he said that the foreign minister of Croatia, Mate Granic, had suggested that the Lasva Valley might become a protected area. He also said that if the ABiH -- if the Armija continued with the offensive, the Bosnian Croats had no alternative but to force two corridors for survival, from Gornji Vakuf up to Novi Travnik, north to Novi Travnik, and from Kiseljak across to Busovaca, by military or political means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We come now to the end of January of 1994. There are two documents in the stack to look at. One is 1364, and the other one is 1364.6. If we look at 1364.6 and if you just give it a glance first, just explain what you can about this document, which I think you produced yesterday yourself.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: The second one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about it? You produced it.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, the reason why this is a slightly odd-looking document, without any top or tail, is because, as I said before, I used to type out these reports of meetings on my laptop, put them on a disk, and then bring them down to my Deputy to put onto the main reports. Unfortunately, there's a gap in the reports that we can get hold of -- that I've been able to get hold of, and I cannot find the actual report which this forms part of. But in manuscript, I've written at the top "30th of January." I know it is mine because it is certainly my style, and in particular I remember the remark towards the bottom of the second page: When asked if the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna would join Croatia, Kordic replied that if that were to happen, the Serbs would join Serbia. On the other hand, he said, "If the Muslims announced their independence, we would suddenly not join China." So that is a phrase which stuck in my mind. That is certainly my document, but the precise date I cannot confirm. But it must have been the 30th of January or one day either side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is, in fact, a fortnight's period at this time which we, I think, have no ECMM documents ourselves, and I can't therefore help further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we come back to the first of the two documents, 1364, and checking first whose report it is, whose report is this? It's not got a name at the foot of it.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: This is a report written from the headquarters in Zagreb. This would have been the daily amalgamation of all the regions' reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go to the second page, paragraph 6, the reference to ECMM DHOM visit, tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. This was the Dputy Head of Mission Operations visited Travnik. By then it was the Greeks, the Greeks were in the Presidency, and we had a meeting with Dario Kordic and -- sorry, do you want --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go on. First of all, were you present yourself?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, I was present. I was present, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, yes, please do go on, looking at paragraph 6, and tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, we had an interesting discussion. Dario Kordic stressed the historical rights in Central Bosnia, and, well, in fact it was really -- it was not a meeting of enormous substance. It was more the Deputy Head of Mission Operations was obtaining information. But I do remember a long spiel from Dario Kordic about the historical rights of the Croats in Central Bosnia and blaming the Muslims for their current breakdowns. And we had another long discussion about Islamic fundamentalism and an Islamic state in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not sure whether you are going to come back to the document 1364.6, but I had wanted to ask the witness something more about the origin and the provenance of that document. Do you intend to come back to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am certainly coming back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll wait until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I only raised it at the same time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice. Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- can't be absolutely sure. Right. I have to go through all of that again, for the record. Yes, I am coming back to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you do come back to it, I'll raise the issue that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were looking at document 1364, the document of the 28th of January, General, and I think we'd covered pretty nearly all I wanted you to tell us about. But looking at that first sheet. Amongst other complaints that Kordic's reported as making, was the selected distribution of aid organised by UNHCR? Was that a recurring theme on one side or both?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It was a recurring theme, and the complaints mainly came from the Croat side. His complaints were that the bulk of humanitarian aid was going to the Bosniaks, and that the humanitarian aid was in fact feeding the ABiH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, now, that meeting, although reported by someone else, and in the body of it identifying ECMM DHOM, was in fact a meeting at which you were present?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have a direct recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I have a direct recollection of the Greek, the Deputy Head of Mission visiting, and we travelled around and had various meetings, and this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We turn now to 1364.6, which you dealt with to a degree already, and which is typed, save for the fact that in the top right corner there's writing. The original's red biro, recording the 30th of January, '94. Whose writing is that?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is my writing. That is my writing. And when I ran this document off, I jotted the date at the top. But, as I say, it clearly was an input for a larger report, for probably our daily or weekly report, but, unfortunately, I cannot find a copy of the final report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just state for the record that the first time we saw this document was in Court today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution have said that they were handed it, I think, yesterday. So that explains the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that I wanted to raise with the witness is whether he can offer any explanation as to why it didn't find its way into the main report, as the other reports did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I deal with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, the physical provenance of the piece of paper that you brought to the Tribunal yesterday. Where had that been kept, until you brought it to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I had kept some of my papers from Bosnia days, but of course this is a long time ago now. A lot of the reports, and so on, I have not retained. This I did not have when I had my first interview by the investigators, but I subsequently found it in amongst my papers. And, as I say, although it is not part of a larger report, it was clearly an input for a larger report, and was written by me, as I say, because it is my style of writing and, as I say, I particularly recall the remark about China.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make quite clear, the writing, 30 January '94, in red biro, was that something that you wrote or judge you must have written contemporaneously, or something that you wrote later?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I wrote it at the time or later on, when I was trying to sort out my papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it something that you wrote in the last few days --

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that we understand the position, this was amongst your papers, which you retained after you left Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Of course, an awful lot of water has flown under the bridge since those days, and I have not retained all my papers, because there's been a lot of other things going on. But when I was going through my papers, in between my interview with the investigators and coming here, I found this document. And I thought it might be of use, so I brought it with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask Sir Martin, were you able to find other documents of this kind, which you had done on your laptop but which didn't find its way into a main report?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I think, no. I think all the others found their way into the main reports, but, as I said, we appear to have a gap, I think it is about a fortnight, about this time, where we do not seem to be able to find the ECMM reports of that period. Unfortunately, it spans this particular period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you are saying it hasn't found its way into a report, or when that's been suggested, is that necessarily the case, or is it possible that it did find its way into a report, but that the report itself simply hasn't been turned up?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I'm quite certain this would have found its way into a report because it is of sufficient significance. It wouldn't have just been left. It would have found itself into a report, either a daily report or a weekly report, or another document we used to produce, which was called a weekly assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I need hardly add, before I come to the next question, that of course our efforts to find missing ECMM documents continue. We had an example, I think, last week of a particular document that I explained we were seeking from another country. But although they were widely distributed, there do appear to be some gaps that we cannot fill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question, General, is this: The document itself has some references that might enable us to fix its date, whether to coincide with the date the 30th of January or otherwise. For example, if you look in the middle of the first page, there's a reference to Kordic spoke about the Dubravica body exchange, which he said he hoped would take place that day. Now, at the moment, have you been able to identify the day or date of a Dubravica body exchange?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: In my appointments diary, appointments diary, I've got down, "Body exchange noted on the 1st of February," which, of course, is two days later than this. Now, that could be the date on which it was postponed to or it could have been about the date on which it was originally planned. So I cannot explain the difference between the 1st of February, which I've noted down "body exchange," and this date of the 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could explore that just one degree further, you don't actually have your appointments diary with you, but when you produced this document yesterday and issues of its date arose, you telephoned back to England and asked your wife to investigate the diary?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I asked my wife to dig up my appointments diary, which I still retained, which, of course, has just got -- it doesn't have notes of meetings; it's just got appointments. And she could not find this, but she noted she found "body exchange" noted for the 1st of February. But as I say, it is possible that that body exchange might have been the postponed date or it might have been the original date, in which case this "30th of January" may not be 100 per cent correct and it might read "1st of February." I'm afraid I cannot explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to your method of preparing documents of this type when you had had an interview or discussion with someone, in this case Kordic, did you make any handwritten notes at the time that you spoke to people, or subsequently in a car or other vehicle, or did you make the -- have the interview or discussion and then come back and type the document up back wherever you were living?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I would normally make brief notes, but I tried not to be writing continuously because I always felt that detracted from a good exchange. So I used to rely on -- a certain amount on notes and memory and then going back and writing it immediately while it was completely fresh in my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by that method, as we can see from the very first sentence of this typed-up note, Kordic explained himself and his position to you, and perhaps you would tell us what that was.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. He said he was the -- he was the Deputy Chief Of Staff or Head Of Staff of the HVO and came third in the order of military seniority, i.e., below Roso, who was the head of the HVO, and General Petkovic, who was the Chief Of Staff and Vice-President of the HDZ for the Croatian Republic, which meant Vice-President of Mate Boban. He also said he was a Member of the House of Representatives. And with him, as usual, was Mr. Ignac Kostroman, who was introduced as the General Secretary of the HDZ, and Kostroman was also a Member of the House of Representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can, of course, read the document in full rather than take time going over it here, but a couple of passages worthy of some note, or perhaps. At the foot of the -- at the end of the second paragraph on the first page, there is a recording of the complaint about the distribution of humanitarian aid, and then on the next paragraph, the Dubravica body exchange, in respect of which Kordic said that the BiH had placed obstructions. Do you have any recollection, one way or another, of an exchange in which there were obstructions or in which it was --

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, these -- this was just outside Vitez, Dubravica. There was a fierce engagement between the Croats and the Bosniaks, allegations of atrocities, and we tried extremely hard, together with the British Battalion, to get into no man's land and clear the bodies and exchange the bodies. There was a delay on the Bosniak side, and I cannot recall -- we did resolve it eventually, but I cannot recall how long it took to resolve, but several days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we scan to read the paragraph at the foot of the first page and the second two paragraphs -- the top two paragraphs on the second page, can you, while we are scanning it, perhaps summarise what Mr. Kordic was saying about the influence of Islam and Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, he was -- he was explaining again the concern that the Croats had about the aims of the Bosniaks, and the warnings about Islamic fundamentalism, and the support that the Bosniaks were receiving from certain Arab or Muslim countries in the world, encouraging them to form a Muslim state in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then on the second page again, the second-to-last paragraph is the paragraph that you've already spoken of and which you remembered directly, that is, the statement where he spoke of not joining China. Underneath that, he said that the military aims of BiH was to have a large part -- a large Muslim Republic, as large as possible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Specifically, he said that the Muslims wanted the Lasva Valley, Zepce, Kiseljak, Makljen Ridge, Prozor, and the Neretva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the last page, he blamed the Mujahedin for roadblocks on Route Diamond, for the robbing of aid convoys; maintained that an Iranian had been killed the day before at Zepce, and concluded -- or at least the report of the interview concludes with Kordic saying that the Croats wished no harm to the Muslims, but they had a right to defend themselves, he explaining that his own family lived in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 44. For what was happening in January and early February of 1994, we actually go to a later document, which is why it's, to this extent, out of date order. It's Document Z1419, the next in the stack. This, General, is, I think, your end-of-tour report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was prepared in April of 1994?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, and I completed it shortly after leaving Zenica, when I was down in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The topic I would like you to deal with is January and February '94 and any reports of HV presence in the area. We can find reference to that on the second page of the document at paragraphs 10 and 14.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. In late January and early February, we started receiving reports of HV, that's Croatian Army forces, moving into Bosnia and Herzegovina to support the HVO. There were many denials, but we had many sightings, and I myself sighted many HV convoys moving up the mountain road from Tomislavgrad to Prozor. They were mostly without number plates, but the HV insignia was clearly visible. Prlic had admitted, in fact, that there were HV troops in Croatia, but he said these were merely some 2.600 volunteers who were born in Bosnia and had returned to defend what he called their country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw these convoys yourself, apart from the lack of number plates and so on, what did they look like? Did they look like vehicles just acting as buses carrying people, or did they look like military units, or what?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: No, many of them were transporters, some were carrying soldiers, some were towing mortars or artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then paragraph 10 on the same page, further up. Just a comment about Praljak and Roso. First of all, what was Praljak's background?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Praljak's background was mainly in the theatre and in the media, and happened to be a great lover of Shakespeare. He handed over to General Roso, who was a soldier's soldier, and had served for many years in the French foreign legion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Praljak's nationality, insofar as you knew it?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, paragraph 45, you learned of the election of Ivan Bender, and also of others to the parliament?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. Philip Watkins, who by then was down in Mostar as the head of the coordinating centre down there, attended a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna parliamentary session on the 17th of February, when Ivan Bender was elected President of the parliament, and Dario Kordic was elected one of the three Vice-Presidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document, 1385, which is a daily report for the 21st of February, and it's signed off Eric Bailo?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. He was acting then as our Operations Officer, responsible for compiling the daily report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second sheet, with lots of underlining on it, speaks of a visit by a Commanding Officer of BritBat to discuss -- with the head of UNHCR and others, to discuss the question of freedom of movement of UNHCR and UNPROFOR convoys. We can again scan read the underlined passage, maybe, and you can tell us, because you were there, what the meeting was about and who conducted it.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes. It was a meeting which was instigated by the CO, Commanding Officer of the British Battalion, in conjunction with the head of UNHCR. And the main aim was to protest strongly about the action of the Croat authorities in Central Bosnia, with increasing restrictions on UNHCR and other convoys and movement. And so it was fundamentally a strong protest about freedom of movement and restrictions and obstructions to the UNHCR convoys coming up into Central Bosnia. But it also raised the subject of the movement of casualties from Stari Vitez, and complained about the linkage between the movement of casualties from Stari Vitez to the supply of water to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was present on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We had evidence about this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kordic's position, in your judgement, in this meeting, in relation to those with whom he was attending?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: It was clear that Blaskic was President, but it was clear that it was Dario Kordic who was leading on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour said, we've had the detail and we needn't go into that anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About this time, did you learn of the resignation of Boban?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that Mate Boban had resigned his position, but Dario Kordic was clearly still the man very much in charge in Central Bosnia, although Ivo Lozancic, the President of the HVO Zepce, was emerging into prominence on the political scene, but it was still Dario Kordic as the leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next and last document, 1417. The 13th of April of '94. A daily report for the 13th of April, the last sheet. So it shows that it's a report by Mr. Stutt. It deals with a meeting of, I think, Mr. Stutt, is it, with Father Bozo?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: I think it was a meeting -- no, one of his teams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Summarise what happened there.

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: He met Father Bozo --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to me that the document speaks for itself. Obviously, this was prepared by a monitor. Sir Martin has no personal knowledge of it; he is just reciting what the document says, and that appears to me to be a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this a matter in which we may well be getting direct evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may be getting direct evidence. It's a question of whether it's more helpful to have the context now than later, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, why don't we wait until we get the witness here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Passing from that document, then to this: Did Mile Plujic at some stage have an exchange with you, that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: When I was down in Mostar with the EU administration, when the indictments against Dario Kordic and Tihomir Blaskic were issued, I think in November 1994, we had an advisory council meeting. And afterwards, Mile Plujic, who was then the President of the Mostar HDZ, came up to me, and he was clearly very angry about the indictments, protesting most strongly, and he produced a phrase, which I remember, which was, "You have got to remember that Kordic was our Churchill." That, to me, was a very significant remark. It clearly indicated the respect in which Kordic was held by the Croats, but it also indicated to me the stature that he held throughout the Croats, particularly, of course, for his role in Central Bosnia. I always had been of the view that Dario Kordic was extremely close to Mate Boban. I'd always believed that he was related by marriage, but I have no proof of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, I think, although you may have covered this already, throughout the conflict, in your judgement, what, if any, practical or real positions did he have in relation to military matters?

utterances.speaker: SIR MARTIN GARROD
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, in Bosnia the military and political were extremely closely intertwined.
